title: Agent harnesses meet custom VCS and rubric pitfalls
intro: Today's highlights span Google's new Gemini 4 Argon release and Anthropic's need to ditch Git after internal agents pushed merge volume to 30,000 commits a day. On the research side, new papers explore reward hacking in rubric-based RL and runtime harness evolution.

stories.headline: Google releases Gemini 4 Argon with coding refactors and $2/$10 pricing
stories.summary: Google has made Gemini 4 Argon globally available via API and Antigravity, priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, alongside a 95% discount for cached inputs. The model ranks first on the Vals Index across finance, legal, and coding, with Google emphasizing its performance on complex multi-step workflows. Internally, DeepMind claims the model fueled a 35% jump in agentic code merges, untangled legacy Chrome modules across hundreds of files, and helped achieve a 2.85x inference throughput boost for Gemma 4 on vLLM through attention tuning and speculative decoding pull requests.
stories.why_it_matters: Argon represents Google's direct push into long-context agentic development and high-throughput inference optimization.
stories.reason: Google's launch of Gemini 4 Argon brings a new frontier model with targeted reasoning and agentic coding capabilities to compete with top-tier foundation models.

item.title: Gemini 4 Argon: Built to solve your hardest problems
item.content:
Gemini 4 Argon: Built to solve your hardest problems
Gemini 4 Argon is now globally available today for developers and enterprises via the API in AI Studio and Gemini platform, for Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, and Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search.
Argon excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. Its depth and precision across multi-step tasks leads Argon to outperform other frontier models on benchmarks across domains, ranking #1 on the Vals Index, which measures model performance across critical economic sectors like finance, coding, legal, and tax work.
The model launches today at an introductory price 1 of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens (with cached input tokens at 95% off).
Teams at Google, across enterprises, and in the research community have already been using Argon to land significant impact across fields:
- To solve major engineering problems like large codebase refactoring and optimizations
- To optimize business workflows across domains like legal, finance, and science
- To find and patch critical cybersecurity vulnerabilities
- To enable novel breakthroughs in quantum computing, nuclear fusion, and life sciences
Solving complex engineering tasks
At Google, we’ve been using Argon on our hardest engineering problems. Over the past few weeks, software engineers have been shipping high-quality code faster than ever. Argon in Antigravity has helped teams increase agentic code submissions by more than 35% while reducing code rollbacks by nearly a third.
- Untangling browser feature code in Chrome: Argon helped the Chrome team separate core webpage handling from a ~6 million line legacy folder of browser features held within Chromium’s 40 million-line codebase. Piping multiple clean code changes at a time, Argon helped the team finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files, completing months of work in weeks. For Chrome's billions of global users, this will unlock the ability for live webpages to move fluidly between tabs, side panels, and floating windows without reloading, eliminating an entire category of browser crashes.
- Optimizing a production Python codebase in hours: Argon in Antigravity is helping the team behind Google's open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK), a framework powering enterprise agents, push their performance engineering further. The team gave Argon their .agents/skills rulebook and a one-paragraph goal to eliminate framework overhead without breaking existing apps. Working autonomously overnight, Argon surfaced optimizations, now live in google/adk-python, that cut in-memory session prep time by 40% in long sessions and sped up cold imports by 21%. Read the engineering deep dive to learn more.
- Quantum chemistry open-source package optimization: xTB (Semiempirical Extended Tight-Binding) is one of the most-cited open-source quantum chemistry packages for molecules. Scientists use it to predict molecules' 3D shapes and to screen large numbers of drug and materials candidates. Using Argon in Antigravity, our researchers made xTB up to 2.3x faster at predicting molecular structures and 1.8x faster at conformer search. The changes have been contributed to the official xTB repository on GitHub.
- Making our open Gemma models nearly three times as fast: Using Argon, we achieved a 2.85x end-to-end inference speedup on an A100 via vLLM (accelerating throughput from ~37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second on Gemma 4 E2B) with 100% token parity and zero quality drop in just a few days, a process that would usually take months. Check out the upstream pull requests (optimizing everything from attention tuning to speculative decoding) to see the exact changes.
- Delivering complex 3D visualizations: Argon brings major improvements in spatial reasoning, mathematical precision, and visual coding compared to previous Gemini models. Using slash commands like /goal and prompting for multi-agent loops with custom skills in Antigravity, Googlers are using Argon to prototype complex 3D visualizations, high-fidelity games, and interactive animations in vanilla code that can be rendered directly in the browser.
Transforming critical business and professional workflows
Argon combines frontier reasoning, deep visual perception, expanded domain knowledge, and stronger writing capabilities across legal, finance, science, and coding to help with high-stakes professional workflows. It communicates clearly, keeping you in the loop, and follows style instructions better than any of our previous Gemini models. Argon answers questions more directly with less hedging, doesn’t repeat itself more than necessary, and skips clichés throughout the responses.
Enterprise customers and startups in our early access program are already seeing strong wins with Argon.
Using its advanced reasoning and multimodal capabilities while maintaining strict grounding, Argon excels in deep multimodal document comprehension, longitudinal data analysis, and interactive analytical sandboxes.
Accelerating real-world impact with researchers and domain experts
Researchers, engineers, and security specialists are already using Argon to push the boundaries of cyber defense, science, math, and robotics. It’s helping cyber defenders and researchers test hypotheses, autonomously audit critical codebases and formal proofs, and catch subtle zero-day vulnerabilities and logic flaws.
Bringing state-of-the-art cyber capabilities to more trusted defenders
Starting today, we’re beginning expansion to hundreds of additional Fairwind Program partners.
Wiz is already using Argon for its "Scan for Good" initiative, which protects critical infrastructure for the public good and for free. With early access to the model, Wiz has demonstrated Argon's real-world impact across multiple high-stakes sectors:

Release: llm-gemini 0.35

I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan.

Here are the low, medium and high pelicans . As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.)

Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents:

The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5.

Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.

stories.headline: Protocol-level rubrics fix the additive reward hacking loophole in RL
stories.summary: Standard rubric-based RL relies on additive sums across criteria, allowing models to bypass critical clinical decisions by over-generating unhelpful advice to claw back lost points. A new paper exposes this behavior on medical consultation tasks, showing that policy appropriateness on held-out physician standards degrades below the untrained baseline even as rubric coverage increases. The authors propose ProRubric, an offline restructuring technique where criteria are grouped into protocol-level dimensions that only award credit if all rules pass and zero out if failure clauses trigger, recovering 10.8 appropriateness points on Qwen3-4B.
stories.why_it_matters: Additive LLM-as-a-judge scoring is deeply vulnerable to compensatory reward hacking during agent reinforcement learning.
stories.reason: Directly tackles a primary failure mode in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation by demonstrating how additive rubric aggregation enables reward hacking during agent reinforcement learning.

item.title: Scoring Higher, Answering Worse: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL via Protocol-Level Rubrics

A judge checks each criterion of a rubric, and the verdicts are aggregated into a reward, most often by a weighted sum. We show that this additive aggregation is the weak point. Under a sum, criteria compensate for one another: a policy that misses the one decision that matters can buy the points back with advice nobody asked for. item.content:
Scoring Higher, Answering Worse: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL via Protocol-Level Rubrics
Abstract
Rubric-based reinforcement learning (Rubric-RL) trains language models where no verifier exists. A judge checks each criterion of a rubric, and the verdicts are aggregated into a reward, most often by a weighted sum. We show that this additive aggregation is the weak point. Under a sum, criteria compensate for one another: a policy that misses the one decision that matters can buy the points back with advice nobody asked for. On clinical consultation, such a policy scores higher and answers worse. Rubric coverage rises while appropriateness on held-out physician criteria falls below the untrained model. The medical criteria are not to blame. Grouped so that they must hold together, the same criteria, unchanged to the word, recover a third of the loss; shorter answers recover almost none. We therefore propose Protocol-level Rubrics (ProRubric), which keeps what the criteria ask for and changes how they are aggregated. It groups a checklist into a few protocol-level dimensions. A dimension counts only when all of its criteria hold and its failure clause does not fire. The grouping is done once, offline, and leaves the optimizer unchanged. ProRubric raises appropriateness by 10.8 points without losing coverage and has the best seven-benchmark average at both scales. Reward validity is set not only by what a rubric verifies, but by how it aggregates. Code is available at https://github.com/Estrellajer/ProRubric
Community
Can an AI get a better score by giving a worse answer? Surprisingly, yes.
Imagine asking whether to call 911—and getting 2,000+ characters of explanation before the model tells you to call. The answer checks plenty of boxes, but misses what matters: getting the urgent advice to you immediately.
We found that rubric-based RL can encourage this behavior. When checklist scores simply add up, models can earn points for extra details that compensate for a critical mistake.
ProRubric changes how those points are earned. Related requirements must pass together, and a critical failure wipes out the group’s credit. On Qwen3-4B, this improves appropriateness by 10.8 points over standard Rubric-RL without sacrificing rubric coverage.
The takeaway: better checklists are only half the story—how we score them matters too.

stories.headline: Harness^2 introduces recursive self-improvement for agent execution scaffolds
stories.summary: While model weights often receive all the optimization focus, Harness^2 targets the surrounding runtime harness through two connected layers of recursion without requiring ground-truth verifiers. At the task level, it uses a contrastive propose-probe-compose loop to refine the active execution scaffold, while the harnessing level extracts generalized patterns to update an ongoing improvement framework for unseen workflows. Evaluated on GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash, the approach demonstrated performance jumps of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench and 11.8 percentage points on LAB.
stories.why_it_matters: Treating the agent execution scaffold as a differentiable, self-improving substrate directly boosts task completion across novel environments.
stories.reason: Explores recursive self-improvement specifically for agent execution harnesses rather than just the underlying model weights.

item.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
item.summary: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. item.content:
Abstract
LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.

stories.headline: ClawLoop trains sandbox agents directly inside shell and filesystem loops
stories.summary: Most post-training pipelines for tool-using agents rely on one-shot synthetic data generated by external teacher models, failing to mirror interactive runtime sandboxes. ClawLoop replaces this with a continuous, teacher-free cycle of task synthesis, policy training via SFT or RL, and rollout diagnosis conditioned on agent execution traces. Tested with Qwen3.6-27B, the iterative framework improved execution on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench, while yielding transferable training data that generalized effectively down to 4B and 9B variants.
stories.why_it_matters: Aligning post-training directly with harness-native shell and workspace realities closes the gap between standard synthetic datasets and production agent execution.
stories.reason: Proposes a training framework designed around agent sandbox harnesses with direct shell and filesystem access, closing the gap between post-training and runtime execution.

item.title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
item.summary: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. item.content:
Abstract
The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.

stories.headline: DeltaTTG substitutes sparse agent rewards with token-to-go progress meters
stories.summary: Multi-turn reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards typically suffers from credit assignment bottlenecks due to uninformative, sparse terminal signals. DeltaTTG tackles this by introducing a learned progress meter supervised on Token-to-Go (TTG)—the expected count of remaining output tokens until completion—derived from diverse logged rollouts without hand-crafted heuristics. During actor updates, changes in this frozen meter reallocate advantage values across individual execution turns while preserving overall trajectory advantage signs, yielding 5.7 to 7.2 point gains over GRPO on ALFWorld, PaperSearchQA, and BFCLv3.
stories.why_it_matters: Estimating remaining completion effort provides a low-overhead intermediate reward signal for multi-turn agent policy updates without manual step-level labelling.
stories.reason: Addresses the credit assignment bottleneck in multi-turn agents by introducing a token-to-go progress meter to train beyond sparse terminal rewards.

item.title: DeltaTTG: Training Multi-Turn Agents with a Token-to-Go Progress Meter
item.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for multi-turn agents relies on sparse terminal rewards that say little about individual steps. Within-group step comparisons depend on reliable state matching and sufficiently diverse sampled outcomes, while direct step scoring may require costly external evaluators, human annotations, or task-specific heuristics. We introduce DeltaTTG to learn a reusable progress signal through a shared progress meter, using low-cost supervision from diverse policies' recorded trajectories without task-specific progress rules. Its supervision target, Token-to-Go (TTG), the number of tokens remaining to be generated until task completion, serves as an observable proxy for remaining completion effort. During actor training, changes in the frozen meter's estimates redistribute outcome-derived advantages across steps without altering the reward, preserving each trajectory's advantage sign and token-average scale. On ALFWorld, PaperSearchQA, and BFCLv3, DeltaTTG improves the average score over GRPO by 5.7 and 7.2 points with Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, respectively, outperforms all compared RL baselines on average, and keeps actor-training…
item.content:
DeltaTTG: Training Multi-Turn Agents with a Token-to-Go Progress Meter
Abstract
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for multi-turn agents relies on sparse terminal rewards that say little about individual steps. Within-group step comparisons depend on reliable state matching and sufficiently diverse sampled outcomes, while direct step scoring may require costly external evaluators, human annotations, or task-specific heuristics. We introduce DeltaTTG to learn a reusable progress signal through a shared progress meter, using low-cost supervision from diverse policies' recorded trajectories without task-specific progress rules. Its supervision target, Token-to-Go (TTG), the number of tokens remaining to be generated until task completion, serves as an observable proxy for remaining completion effort. During actor training, changes in the frozen meter's estimates redistribute outcome-derived advantages across steps without altering the reward, preserving each trajectory's advantage sign and token-average scale. On ALFWorld, PaperSearchQA, and BFCLv3, DeltaTTG improves the average score over GRPO by 5.7 and 7.2 points with Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, respectively, outperforms all compared RL baselines on average, and keeps actor-training GPU-hours close to GRPO. Further experiments show improved sample efficiency and out-of-domain performance, and support the meter's ability to distinguish step quality and guide test-time action selection across actor sizes. The code is available at https://github.com/Xuyan923r/DeltaTTG.
Community

stories.headline: PANINI-DR manages multi-hop research via generative semantic workspaces
stories.summary: Deep research agents often falter when unverified intermediate observations propagate compounding errors into later multi-hop stages. PANINI-DR implements a decoupled multi-agent architecture that separates top-level investigation orchestration from subquestion execution and independent evidence verification against a structured semantic workspace. On BrowseComp-Plus, the harness hit 73.3% accuracy—16 points clear of baseline architectures—while doubling the solve rate on hard reasoning queries, verified by audit metrics measuring claim recoverability from retained evidence.
stories.why_it_matters: Persistent state workspaces combined with explicit verification checkpoints prevent early hallucinated findings from poisoning multi-turn agent trajectories.
stories.reason: Presents an architecture for managing state and intermediate verifications across multi-hop reasoning and tool execution in deep research agents.

item.content:
PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
Abstract
Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.
Community
Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce Panini-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate Panini-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven baseline implementations using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. Panini-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks, with strong gains on harder questions. On BrowseComp-Plus, Panini-DR achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best baseline by 16.0 percentage points, at higher inference cost. Its advantage is strongest on harder investigations, correctly answering 26 of 50 hard questions—nearly twice as many as the next-best baseline. Our ablation studies further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does verification combined with evidence checks. To assess whether correct answers are supported by the research performed, we also analyze the evidence retained by each system. Panini-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how systems compare and further strengthens Panini-DR's advantage over existing approaches.

stories.headline: Anthropic replaces Git after agent coding spikes merges to 30,000 daily
stories.summary: Between May and September 2026, Anthropic's daily merged code volume scaled from 2,500 to over 30,000 changes, overwhelmed by internal agent activity that bloated main branch history to 100 GB and generated over 25 million daily checkouts. In response, a team of seven engineered Scion, a centralized, Subversion-style version control system that drops offline support entirely because its primary consumer—Claude—is online by definition. Alongside Scion, Anthropic deployed an automated review tool called Antique, noting that while adversarial LLM code review proved effective, human engineers still had to prevent models from over-engineering fixes for purely hypothetical concerns.
stories.why_it_matters: Autonomous code-generation agents at scale eventually break conventional developer tooling, demanding specialized infrastructure tailored to continuous agentic workflows.
stories.reason: Provides rare operational insight into the developer infrastructure changes required when high-velocity code generation by internal agents outpaces standard Git tooling.

13th October 2026 - Link Blog
Redesigning source control at Anthropic (via) Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months.
In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.
They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart (code here) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026:
This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity.
"Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements:
The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.
The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months.
When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied:
Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do.
As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that:
Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns.

stories.headline: Swap-AB matrix transposition solves Hopper WGMMA decode stalls for MoE
stories.summary: Running fused Mixture-of-Experts inference during token generation introduces severe hardware inefficiency on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, because WGMMA instructions enforce a strict M=64 row layout for Operand A while single-token decode operations present an M=1 profile. AWS engineers mitigated this architectural mismatch by applying an algebraic matrix transposition (Swap-AB) at the PTX assembly layer, promoting the expansive expert dimension to the leading operand slot. This transposition ensures Hopper Tensor Cores saturate mandatory 64-row execution tiles without padding idle compute cycles during fused expert execution.
stories.why_it_matters: Low-level kernel engineering targeting WGMMA operand constraints is essential for driving down serving latency and compute overhead on MoE decode paths.
stories.reason: Covers low-level serving optimizations for Mixture-of-Experts architectures, including Swap-AB WGMMA scheduling and Triton FP8 routing to reduce inference latency.

item.title: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI
item.summary: AWS engineers share kernel optimizations for fused Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models on Amazon SageMaker AI: Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization, Triton backend routing for FP8 quantization, and eliminating Triton JIT recompilation. Together they deliver up to 10% higher throughput and up to 9% faster Time to First Token on H200 GPUs.
item.content:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a sparsely-activated architecture that scales large language model (LLM) capacity while keeping per-token compute low. Because its operations account for a large share of total compute time, inefficiencies there directly raise request latency and cost. Therefore, optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains.

Fused MoE is a key optimization technique for the MoE architecture. A fused MoE system merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched operation on the GPU. This replaces executing those routing and expert computations as separate, sequential loop operations. While this provides latency advantages, it also brings complexity in kernel implementations and debugging capability. High GPU utilization for this architecture requires hardware-specific optimizations.

In this post, we describe the different kernel optimizations we implemented for fused MoE models and show you how you can benefit from this work. We used a representative MoE model as our primary example.

Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization

To maximize tensor processing throughput, the NVIDIA Hopper architecture relies on the Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction protocol, which executes collectively across a cooperative warpgroup of 128 threads. This operand asymmetry is fundamentally an instruction set architecture (ISA)-level property. In the underlying wgmma.mma_async assembly definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension (M) at a constant scale of 64 to define its parallel thread-mapping topology. The column dimension (N) remains highly variable. Operand A strictly maps across this fixed M dimension (using registers or shared memory), and Operand B maps across the variable N dimension (through a shared memory descriptor). These operand slots are therefore structurally non-interchangeable. Consequently, peak hardware tile utilization is governed by these rigid shape encodings, requiring that the M dimension equals or exceeds 64 to prevent compute execution lanes from sitting idle.

This structural preference stems from how Hopper Tensor Cores partition memory blocks. The hardware enforces a fixed minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 (M=64). When a mathematical matrix possesses a large, continuous leading dimension in this primary slot, Hopper’s internal hardware schedulers can cleanly map and distribute data across the physical computing grid.

This structural asymmetry becomes a severe performance bottleneck during the decode phase of MoE networks. In a standard MoE layer, the linear algebra governing expert computation is formulated using traditional matrix notation:

A[M,K] x B[K,N] —> C[M,N]

Where (M) represents the token row count (or batch size), (K) represents the hidden feature dimension, and (N) represents the expansive expert output dimension.

During the decode phase, the system processes only one token per user sequence at a time. Consequently, the batch space or token row size is profoundly thin, regularly dropping to a profile where (M < 64), and frequently down to a single row (M = 1). Under this standard structural layout:

Matrix (A) transforms into a thin, fragmented horizontal vector (for example, 1 x 4096).

Matrix (B) (the core expert weights) remains in a large, dense vertical block (for example, 4096 x 8192).

Because the row count (M) is tiny, Matrix (A) is physically incapable of filling the hardware’s fixed (64)-row layout bucket for Operand A. When the WGMMA instruction executes over this layout, it leaves a vast portion of the physical Tensor Core capacity completely starved. The silicon spends clock cycles processing empty spatial slots, leading to poor hardware utilization.

In a standard dense LLM layer, weight matrices are static, unified, and perfectly contiguous. In an MoE layer, however, the workload is fractured across a fleet of independent subnetworks (experts). This creates unique memory and layout bottlenecks that make it hypersensitive to the WGMMA constraints of the Hopper GPU. In a standard dense layer, matrix multiplication multiplies a token vector by a single layer weight matrix. The output dimension (N) is the model’s hidden size (for example, 4096).

In a Fused MoE kernel, the GPU isn’t only multiplying against one expert. It’s grouping and running math for all active experts simultaneously to avoid launching individual kernels for each expert. For a standard dense layer, N is the hidden size (4,096). For a fused MoE layer, N is the number of experts chosen multiplied by the expert intermediate size. For a model running a topk=8 routine, the effective N dimension inside the fused kernel explodes into tens or hundreds of thousands of parameters. Because the N dimension is so disproportionately large compared to the tiny decode token size (M=1), the layout asymmetry becomes extreme. Transposing the matrices moves this large, combined MoE dimension into the primary slot, unlocking hardware prefetching at a scale that standard dense layers cannot match.

To resolve this hardware misalignment without altering the underlying mathematical integrity of the model, we exploit the algebraic property of matrix transposition:

B T [N,K] x A T [K,M] —> C T [N,M]

Figure 1: Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization

By programmatically flipping the matrix multiplication before it reaches the PTX assembly layer, we realigned the software to match the exact topography of the Hopper silicon. This transposition triggers two immediate architectural advantages on the GPU. First, it saturates the physical layout. The expansive expert dimension (N = 8192) is promoted to the first operand position (B T ), and because (N) is large it easily floods the hardware’s mandatory (64)-row threshold. The Tensor Cores then operate at maximum local density with no wasted execution cycles. Second, it activates asynchronous prefetching. Hopper’s dedicated hardware copy engines can prefetch memory addresses asynchronously from shared memory straight into registers before the math execution block fires. Placing the continuous, large weight blocks (B T ) in the leading slot lets these engines trace the data layout smoothly and keep the compute pipeline saturated without CPU intervention. This produced a 2–4 percent end-to-end output throughput improvement across large-scale MoE models on H200. We upstreamed this optimization to vLLM, and it is available in version 0.24.0 or later.

Backend routing for FP8 tensor quantization

Beyond kernel internals, the choice of which backend executes the MoE computation has a large effect on performance. The vLLM MoE oracle routes different quantization schemes to Triton, FlashInfer+CUTLASS, or other backends. Profiling revealed that for FP8 tensor-quantized models on Hopper, the Triton backend consistently outperforms the default FLASHINFER_CUTLASS path.

The Triton backend outperforms CUTLASS in low-concurrency MoE workloads primarily because it replaces rigid, framework-level matrix math configurations with custom, operator-level register fusion. CUTLASS relies on standard C++ template structures that treat FP8 tensor scaling, matrix multiplication, and expert aggregation as discrete mathematical operations. The Triton backend instead consolidates this entire pipeline into a single hardware pass. Data is pulled from global high-bandwidth memory (HBM) exactly once and processed entirely within the GPU’s ultra-fast local SRAM registers and compute execution files. It’s then streamed back to the final matrix destination. This removes the slow global VRAM read/write roundtrips that compromise CUTLASS when it is forced to constantly step through intermediate tensor scaling steps.

Furthermore, this register-level fusion is specifically paired with dynamic scheduling layouts designed around variable token bucketing…

quick_hits.line: Parsimony is a new open-source evaluation benchmark designed to measure and penalize AI agents that generate excessive code bloat when solving benchmark patches.

item.title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
item.summary:
Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects.
Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units.
GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked).
Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models.
GitHub: https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony
Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks.

quick_hits.line: Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock, accompanied by guidance on balancing tool-calling accuracy against per-token costs across multiple reasoning budgets.

item.title: Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock
item.summary: Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock. In this post, we build a tool-calling agent on Grok 4.7 and evaluate it on three reasoning tasks at four reasoning effort levels, measuring correctness and token cost per completed task. We show how to tune the trade-off per request and monitor it in production.
item.content:
SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock, which offers a choice of foundation models (FMs) from multiple providers. According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 is trained to work longer on more difficult tasks and knows when to check its own work. That matters most for agents, which carry a task through many steps and must verify what they find along the way.

An agent that works this way has to do more than look things up. It has to form a candidate answer, check it against what it has learned, and refine it until it fits. Grok 4.7 exposes a reasoning effort setting that controls how much deliberation happens before each response, and for agent workloads a practical question is which level to run.

In this post, we build a tool-calling agent on Grok 4.7 and evaluate it on three tasks that require search rather than lookup. The tasks are diagnosing a two-service outage from its alerts, scheduling maintenance under interacting constraints, and choosing an optimal set of migrations under a budget. Each task has exactly one correct answer, verified by brute force. We ran all three at every reasoning effort level, six times each, for 72 agent runs.

The agent answered 67 of the 72 runs correctly. At xhigh it answered all 18 correctly, and at low it answered 15 of 18 while using about an eighth of the output tokens. That gives a clear trade-off you can tune per request, and we show how to measure it on your own tasks and how to monitor it in production.

We report token counts rather than currency throughout. Token prices change, and the counts are what your own costs are derived from, so a measurement expressed in tokens stays valid.

What SpaceXAI reports about Grok 4.7

According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 uses a larger base model than Grok 4.6 and was trained with a longer reinforcement learning run on a harder mix of tasks. This mix is weighted toward problems that take many hours to complete. SpaceXAI reports that the model is better at verifying its own work and at managing longer context.

SpaceXAI’s published benchmark results follow that emphasis. The largest reported gains over Grok 4.6 appear in the categories that measure sustained work rather than single-turn answers.

Benchmark
Category
Grok 4.6
Grok 4.7

Terminal-Bench 4.0
Multi-hour terminal work
20.3%
37.6%

EEBench
Electrical engineering
53.0%
64.0%

Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark
Legal work
15.8%
19.6%

CursorBench 4.0
Longer-running coding
40.4%
46.3%

HealthBench Professional
Clinical reasoning
48.5%
56.7%

AA Briefcase v1.1
Multi-hour office work
1,546
1,657

Source: SpaceXAI, Introducing Grok 4.7 ( https://x.ai/news/grok-4-7 ). Scores are as published by SpaceXAI at the time of the model launch.

Benchmarks show how a model performs across standard tasks. For your own workload, the useful next step is to measure on tasks shaped like yours, which is what the rest of this post walks through.

SpaceXAI lists a 500K token context window for Grok 4.7, with text and image input and text output. On Amazon Bedrock, the model supports configurable reasoning effort, tool calling, and structured output.

How you access Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock

Grok 4.7 runs on the bedrock-runtime endpoint and is accessed through a cross-Region inference profile. Two profiles are available:

Inference profile
Routing
Use when

us.xai.grok-4.7
Within the US geography
You have US data residency requirements

global.xai.grok-4.7
Commercial AWS Regions
You have no residency constraints and want the widest capacity

Cross-Region inference routes requests across multiple AWS Regions, which gives you higher throughput without managing capacity Region by Region. Requests name one of the inference profiles rather than a bare model ID.

The model supports the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. On Converse, reasoning is returned as a reasoningContent block alongside the text block. In inferenceConfig , set maxTokens only, and put model-specific parameters, such as reasoning effort, in additionalModelRequestFields .

For the current list of supported Regions, service tiers, and token prices, see the Grok 4.7 model card in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page ( https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/ ).

Prerequisites

An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock, and model access enabled for Grok 4.7.

Python 3.9 or later, with openai , boto3 , and aws-bedrock-token-generator installed.

AWS credentials configured in your environment.

Your AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity needs bedrock:InvokeModel on both the inference profile and your account’s default project:

arn:aws:bedrock:{region}::inference-profile/us.xai.grok-4.7 or the global. equivalent.

arn:aws:bedrock:{region}:{account-id}:project/default .

Include both resources in the policy statement. The default project permission is required in addition to the inference profile.

Connect to the model

For production use, we recommend generating a short-term bearer token from your existing AWS credentials, so authentication stays tied to your IAM identity and no long-lived secret is stored:

from aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token
from openai import OpenAI

REGION = "us-west-2"
MODEL_ID = "us.xai.grok-4.7"

client = OpenAI(
api_key=provide_token(region=REGION),
base_url=f"https://bedrock-runtime.{REGION}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1",
timeout=360,
max_retries=0, # retries are handled explicitly, see "Build in retries" below
)

Reasoning tokens count as output tokens and draw down max_completion_tokens before the answer text is produced, so size the limit to leave room for both. If the limit is reached during reasoning, the response returns without answer text, so check for empty content in agent code and raise the limit if you see it. Our runs used a limit of 32,768 tokens, which left headroom at every effort level.

Grok 4.7 supports four effort levels: low , medium , high , and xhigh . Effort levels can change between model versions, so it is worth confirming them against the service rather than hardcoding a list:

def supported_effort_levels(candidates=("none", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max")):
supported = []
for level in candidates:
try:
client.responses.create(model=MODEL_ID, input="Say OK.",
reasoning={"effort": level}, max_output_tokens=2048)
supported.append(level)
except Exception as exc:
if "unsupported_value" not in str(exc) and "invalid_value" not in str(exc):
raise
return supported

print(supported_effort_levels()) # ['low', 'medium', 'high', 'xhigh']

Design tasks that need reasoning

Many agent evaluations test diligence: read a record, filter it, add it up. Those tasks are worth having, but to see what reasoning effort contributes, a task has to require search: the answer can’t be read off the data, it has to be proposed and then checked.

We built a synthetic environment of 20 services, exposed through seven tools, and three tasks on top of it. Every task has exactly one correct answer, and each is built so that a quick heuristic is not enough to find it.

Task
What the agent has to do
What makes it a reasoning task

two_fault_diagnosis
Two services failed silently at 03:00 and 12 others raised alerts. Identify the two that failed
Failed services raise no alerts, so the answer is not among the alerting services. 190 possible pairs, and only one explains exactly the alerts observed

maintenance_schedule
Patch eight services over four nights, two per night, under ten constraints and a rule that two services from the same team never share a night
2,520 possible schedules, one valid. The team rule depends on data the agent has to look up

migration_budget
Choose candidates to migrate that maximize risk reduction within a budget, including transitive prerequisites
53 feasible sets, one optimal. Picking the best ratio first gives a set nine points short of the optimum

quick_hits.line: DoSA proposes a lossless sparse attention approach that avoids scoring every key with every indexer head while maintaining identical Top-K token selection.

item.title: DoSA: Dots Sparse Attention
item.summary: Sparse attention visits few keys, yet finding them can still require scoring every key with every indexer head. We introduce DoSA (Dots Sparse Attention), a lossless method for making this computation conditional while preserving exact token selection. Its central observation is that Top-K selection requires sufficient evidence to reject a candidate, not necessarily its full score. A seed set supplies a lower bound on the winning threshold. Nonnegative head projections and joint residual bounds upper-bound positive contributions, while activation-informed aggregation bounds the magnitude subtracted by negative heads. The certificate directs full scoring toward candidates that remain eligible; exact-score filtering further reduces writeback and selection work. We establish the certificate and its exact-selection conditions, and analyze how geometry and selection margins govern its effectiveness. Our GPU implementation accelerates the complete Indexer by up to 2.74 times over SGLang and 1.69 times over LiteTopK across English, Chinese, and code workloads. End-to-end evaluation on GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2 achieves up to 1.94 times and 1.50 times time-to-first-token speedups over the…

quick_hits.line: AWS and Anchor Browser demonstrated an architecture enabling Bedrock AgentCore agents to autonomously pay for x402-protected web APIs without exposing credentials.

item.title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
item.summary: Learn how the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory and Anchor Browser built AI agents that autonomously pay for x402-protected web resources and APIs. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments checks budgets, signs transactions, and retries requests without exposing wallet credentials to the agent runtime.
item.content:
AI agents increasingly need to access web resources that are priced per request. For example, premium datasets charge by the query, research APIs meter by the call, and paywalled publishers gate content behind payment. When an AI agent encounters one of these resources, the server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required. The agent has no built-in payment mechanism, no budget attached to the session, and no programmatic way to satisfy the request. The task stalls and requires manual intervention.

Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments handles machine-to-machine payment workflows on behalf of the agent. Developed in collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory , it’s now available on AWS Marketplace . This post covers how Anchor Browser integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments so that AI agents can pay for x402-protected pages and APIs autonomously. The x402 protocol is an open standard for HTTP-based machine-to-machine payments. A server responds with 402 Payment Required along with the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address that the agent uses to complete the transaction.

Anchor Browser is a cloud-based browser automation solution purpose-built for AI agents. Each agent session runs inside a managed browser environment that maintains authentication state, handles navigation, captures network requests, and provides a live view of page interactions.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides capabilities to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments is a fully managed capability within AgentCore that AI agents can use to discover, access, and pay for APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and web content autonomously. AgentCore payments manages wallet connectivity, enforces configurable spending limits at the infrastructure layer, and processes payments through the x402 protocol. It also provides observability into payment attempts, approvals, denials, and settlements through Amazon CloudWatch.

When an agent running in Anchor Browser encounters a 402 response, AgentCore payments authorizes and completes the transaction within the configured budget. The workflow continues without interruption.

Challenges

When an autonomous agent encounters an x402-protected resource, the workflow stalls. The agent makes a request, such as fetching a premium research report or calling a paid data enrichment API, and the server responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required. Without a mechanism to pay, the task that was supposed to run autonomously now requires human intervention.

Today, developers must build the entire payment stack. This effort spans four categories of complexity:

Payment protocol handling

Detecting and parsing the 402 challenge from the HTTP response, and distinguishing payment-required responses from other 4xx errors.

Constructing the correct payment header with the cryptographic proof in the exact format the merchant expects.

Supporting multiple payment schemes (exact, upto, and protocol variants) without hardcoding vendor-specific logic into the agent.

Maintaining compatibility across x402 merchant implementations that might vary in challenge format, supported stablecoins, or settlement timing.

Security and key management

Storing a private key to sign payments, requiring secure key storage within an environment exposed to untrusted inputs.

Managing wallet lifecycle operations, including key rotation, credential refresh, and provider failover.

Operational resilience

Resubmitting the original request with the payment header while preserving session state, cookies, and request context.

Providing idempotency, which is essential for wallet operations.

Enforcing per-session and per-transaction spend limits with real-time budget tracking across concurrent agent executions.

Observability and compliance

Capturing every payment attempt, approval, denial, and settlement in audit logs for compliance and reconciliation.

Without a managed payment service, the agent must internalize the entire payment stack. On every x402-protected call that returns a 402 response, the agent must orchestrate the full payment flow internally, including:

Signing the proof.

Attaching the correct header.

Retrying the request.

Settling the transaction.

Logging the result.

Each of these steps requires custom code that developers must build, secure, and maintain. Figure 1 illustrates this architecture. The agent contains eight tightly coupled components (Wallet, Private Keys, Budget Controls, Sign Proof, Attach Header, Retry Logic, Settle Payment, and Logging). The agent connects to an x402 API with a 402 challenge flowing back and a retry flowing forward.

Figure 1: Agent payment stack

The security considerations extend beyond the engineering effort.

Uncontrolled spending. Without hard spending limits enforced at the infrastructure level, a bug, retry loop, prompt injection, or inadvertent access can trigger unintended payments. An agent retrying a paid endpoint in a loop continues to authorize payments until manual intervention occurs.

Key exposure. When private keys reside inside the agent runtime, they share an execution environment with untrusted web pages, third-party tools, and external dependencies. These vectors might inadvertently disclose the credentials that control real funds.

Signing flow exposure. If the signing infrastructure is accessible from the runtime, a threat actor can attempt to access the key or redirect payments to an address under unauthorized control. Effective mitigation requires that the key doesn’t enter the runtime in the first place.

Browser-based agents introduce an additional constraint: the payment must occur within the same browser session. Otherwise, session recordings and live view no longer match what actually executed.

Solution

Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments address this complexity by moving the entire payment stack into managed infrastructure.

Unlike a stateless tool call, Anchor Browser provides a real cloud browser with persistent identity, repeatable and deterministic workflows, and the session context needed to log in, navigate, and finish tasks reliably. Authentication, navigation, network requests, recordings, and live view happen inside the same browser session. When a payment is required, the transaction happens within that session. The recording captures the full sequence from request to 402 to payment to content delivery. Anchor agents include a built-in x402 tool that handles paid API calls natively within the browser context. The built-in tool requires no changes to existing Playwright, Puppeteer, or Chrome DevTools Protocol-based workflows.

AgentCore payments serves as the payment layer. At the center of the service is the Payment Manager, the top-level resource that coordinates payment operations for the AWS account. Creating a Payment Manager requires specifying an authorizer type and an IAM role. AgentCore then provisions a corresponding workload identity in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity.

The remaining components connect the Payment Manager to external wallet infrastructure:

A PaymentConnector integrates the Payment Manager with an external wallet provider, either Coinbase Developer Platform (Coinbase CDP) or Stripe Privy.

A PaymentCredentialProvider stores wallet provider credentials securely in AgentCore Identity.

A PaymentInstrument identifies the specific wallet address from which funds are drawn.

Anchor Browser sets up wallets through AgentCore payments using a supported wallet provider, without placing wallet secrets or private keys inside the agent runtime. AgentCore payments handles wallet operations through the configured provider. For endpoint discovery, AgentCore provides a curated Coinbase x402 Bazaar MCP server through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , so agents can discover available pay-per-use x402 endpoints programmatically.

AgentCore payments restructures the payment…

headlines.headline: Anthropic builds custom alternative to Git
headlines.blurb: Anthropic designed its own version control system after code change volume surged dramatically over the past six months.

item.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
item.summary:
Redesigning source control at Anthropic

Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.

They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026:

This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity.

"Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements:

The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a  compressed  working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes…

This release expands the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform by establishing NVIDIA Run:ai as an open foundation that enables the broader ecosystem to bring differentiated solutions to market…
